b: There are all kinds of reasons why winter is a great time to target bass with crawfish-imitating baits.

For starters, bass like to hang along the rocky bottoms in five to 30 feet, where crawfish are often plentiful in colder months. And as water temps approach 40 degrees, the crawfish become dormant — making them easy meals to pick off. This means that bass, which are also trying to conserve energy, don’t have to strain for a high-protein crawfish meal.
With all of that in mind, let’s look at some of the best craw imitators to fish with this winter.

For those deeper bass relating to crawfish, nothing beats a finesse jig in the winter. These little morsels perfectly mimic a slow-crawling crawfish looking for a hole to hide in. Baits like the Dirty Jigs Weekender Finesse Jig are ideal. These compact jigs are lightweight, typically around half an ounce. They also pair well with a small craw-style trailer — like the Strike King Baby Rage Bug — to perfectly represent the natural color, size, and profile of a crawfish.

Finesse jigs by and large have round, ball-shaped heads that traverse rugged terrain fairly well. But these baits aren’t for grass or wood. Instead, they roll over and through mixtures of chunk rock, gravel, sand, clay, pebbles, and boulders. Just keep a semi-slack tension on your line as you drag the bait through, and be patient. You can typically pop a bait undone if it snags, as long as you don’t errantly snatch and set the hook into the cover.

While you can fish these jigs on spinning gear, it’s typically unnecessary to do so. A casting rod in the 7’ to 7’ 3” medium-heavy/fast range is more capable. Pairing a rod like this with a 7:1 gear ratio reel spooled with 15- to 17-pound test fluorocarbon will give you the ability to make long casts and pull large fish up off the bottom quickly, to remove the threat of your line cutting on the rocks.

Any crankbait that runs less than 12 feet deep is likely to get bit in the winter. But some are definitely better equipped for certain situations. Finesse crankbaits, like the classic Rapala Shad Rap and similar baits, have tight wiggles and work really well throughout the winter in three to 10 feet of water. Squarebills, like the Bandit 100, handle the one- to four-foot stretch well. And then there are the flat-sided cranks, too, like the Strike King Hardliner 35, which is good in the three- to seven-foot range, as well. All of these are great for both fishing in the winter and targeting crawfish-oriented bass.

While bass will eat shad, crawfish, and other forage, color selection is important to truly mimic crawfish. In clear-water scenarios, select darker colors or translucent baits, like many of the popular phantom Wiggle Warts. In more stained and muddier waters, it’s a good idea to use paled-out browns and oranges that glow in sunny conditions. Dark colors, meanwhile, create crisp silhouettes in lowlight and low-visibility situations.

A range of gear works, depending on the crankbait you pick. For light-weight finesse baits that are hard to throw, spinning gear is best. But for medium-diving and shallow crankbaits, casting gear is more capable. Fish these baits around shallow to mid-range rock, wood, and other cover where crawfish like to reside.

The Ned rig is the ultimate cleanup bait, especially in the winter. I remember when this bait first caught on across the country about 10 years ago. It had been the rage for months, but I hadn’t tried it yet and was tired of hearing about it. On one brisk winter day, I tied on a shaky head and a Ned rig to see if the latter really was all that the bass fishing world said it was. I gave equal time to the shaky head and Ned rig, but I surprisingly found that the simple bite-sized Ned rig outperformed the shaky head something like 5 to 1. The exact ratio slips my mind, but it was no contest.

The best bait and jighead combo I’ve found is the Picasso Rhino Ned Head paired with a Z-Man Finesse TRD. This 2.75” soft plastic bait is made of ElaZtech, which means two things: It’s super durable, and it floats. It allows you to rig up one bait that you can use all day. And it also gives the Ned rig a phenomenal, subtle action as the tail floats off the bottom and washes around, even when the bait is stationary.

The Ned rig works best in clear water, and it is a great bait to fish at a wide range of depths. I’ve caught bass on a Ned rig in winter on shallow rock veins that are in less than two feet of water, and I’ve caught them on hard bottom out to 25 feet. You will need to adjust the weight of your jighead accordingly. And, while there are some magnum Ned heads on the market now that are good for summertime ledge fishing, a traditional, light-weight Ned rig works best on spinning gear. A 15-pound braided mainline to 10-pound fluorocarbon leader is typically sufficient, but don’t be afraid to beef that up a bit if you’re targeting large fish in rough terrain.

Whether you’re cranking cold water or slow-crawling a finesse jig or Ned rig, using baits that imitate crawfish in the winter is a surefire way to lure in bass. From catching numbers with the Ned rig to boating big ones with a shallow squarebill, you’ll just need to keep in mind what makes a crawfish-style bait appealing to a bass.

Fish these baits slowly. Pick colors that match the hatch. And make sure you pick baits that allow you to sample a good chunk of the water column — from one to 15 feet, at least. If you do that, you’ll surely find success with crawfish imitators this winter.
